# How AI Works for Kids

> Free, hands-on AI lessons for kids ages 6–10 (roughly grades 1–5). Kids teach a tiny AI named Pip, then test it and fix its mistakes, and learn how real AI learns, guesses, and goes wrong. 15 lessons in two sections, about 95 minutes total, plus a 10-question final quiz. No ads, no accounts, no live chatbot. Made by Nick Castro in Chicago.

Each lesson has four steps: Read (a 5-page picture story with a "Read it to me" button), Play (a hands-on game), Check (two quick questions), and Badge (a light in Pip's brain turns on). Section 1, "Teach Pip" (lessons 1–7), ends with a printable certificate. Section 2, "Pip Grows Up" (lessons 8–15), ends with a 10-question final quiz and a second printable certificate (it unlocks after all Section 2 lessons and the quiz). Section 2 lessons also end with an optional "Try it with a grown-up" mission: a sample prompt a grown-up can type into their own AI account. The site never connects to an AI, and the missions don't recommend any product. Section 1 is suggested first, but nothing is locked.

The games run real, very small models inside the web page: a weighted nearest-neighbor classifier (Sort the Glorbs), a one-clue decision stump trained on the child's examples (Fix Pip's Mix-up), a word-pair counting next-word model (Story Builder), a pixel-matching picture guesser (Pixel Peek), and a nearest-neighbor drawing guesser that kids can teach (Pixel Peek, part 2), a look-alike team picker that leaves out shapes it never saw until kids add examples of every kind (Pick the Team), and a nearest-neighbor sorting machine that kids build, test, fix, and check for every kind (My Sorting Machine). Drawings and kid-built models are never saved or sent. Nothing a child does is sent to an AI service. Progress and the final quiz result (score and missed topic IDs only) are stored only in the browser (localStorage); the quiz is not tracked in analytics. Optional, anonymous Google Analytics may be enabled with ad features off; no personal data is collected from children.

## Lessons

### Section 1: Teach Pip

1. [Meet Pip: What is AI?](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/what-is-ai): AI is a computer program that learns patterns from lots of examples, then makes guesses. Game: AI Detective (find the things in a house that use AI). ~5 min.
2. [Teach by Showing](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/learning-from-examples): AI learns from examples, not a list of rules; more good examples help. Game: Sort the Glorbs (a nearest-neighbor model learns the child's secret rule and shows why it guessed). ~6 min.
3. [How Chatbots Talk](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/guess-the-next-word): Chatbots write by guessing the next word, again and again. Games: Next Word! and Story Builder. ~6 min.
4. [Good Examples In, Good Guesses Out](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/sneaky-clues): Lopsided examples teach AI the wrong clue (bias); better examples fix it. Game: Fix Pip's Mix-up. ~6 min.
5. [Sure Doesn't Mean Right](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/ai-can-be-wrong): AI can sound sure and still be wrong (hallucinations); check with a grown-up or a trusted source. Game: Fact or Fib? ~5 min.
6. [Real or Made by AI?](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/real-or-made-up): AI can make pictures and voices of things that never happened; look closely and ask a grown-up. Game: Spot the Glitches. ~5 min.
7. [Be the Boss of AI](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/smart-and-safe): Keep private things private, remember AI isn't a person, ask a grown-up when unsure. Games: Go, Ask, or Stop and Secret Shield. ~6 min.

### Section 2: Pip Grows Up

8. [Where Did AI Come From?](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/where-did-ai-come-from): A short, kid-level history of AI in general eras (people imagined thinking machines long ago; the name "artificial intelligence" was given about 70 years ago, in the mid-1950s). AI became practical once there was far more data, much faster computers, and better ways of learning from examples. Includes "Meet the AI helpers": ChatGPT (made by OpenAI), Claude (made by Anthropic), Gemini (made by Google), and Grok (made by xAI), listed A to Z, each with the same neutral one-line description ("a chat helper that answers questions and helps with writing"), no ranking and no links, and a reminder that every AI helper can be wrong, so always check. Game: AI Time Machine. ~7 min.
9. [How Pip Sees Pictures](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/how-ai-sees-pictures): Computers see pictures as pixels and look for patterns in them; more pixels help AI guess better. Game: Pixel Peek (guess a hidden picture as pixels appear, then paint a 6x6 pixel picture for Pip to guess and teach it when it's wrong). ~7 min.
10. [Say It Clearly](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/say-it-clearly): A prompt is what you ask an AI; clear details get better results and missing details get filled in with guesses. Game: Monster Maker. ~6 min.
11. [Check It, Fix It](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/check-it-fix-it): Find the mistake, check it in a trusted source, then tell the AI exactly what to fix. Game: Pip's Homework. ~6 min.
12. [AI Can Help You Learn and Make Things](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/ai-learning-helper): Use AI as a helper (quizzes, explanations, ideas), not a doer; your own thinking and making matter. Games: Helper or Doer? and Pip's Idea Machine. ~7 min.

13. [Fair for Everyone](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/fair-for-everyone): If an AI only learns from some kinds of examples, it can leave others out; examples of every kind help make it fair. Uses made-up creatures (Glorbs), not real groups of people. Game: Pick the Team (Pip picks only round Glorbs; kids add square and spiky examples until the Fair Meter balances). ~7 min.
14. [Secrets Stay Safe](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/secrets-stay-safe): What you type to an AI travels to a company's computers and can be saved, so leave out full names, schools, addresses, birthdays, and passwords; safe stand-ins like "my friend" still get good help. Game: Prompt Scrubber. ~7 min.
15. [Build Your Own AI](https://howaiworksforkids.com/lessons/build-your-own-ai): Kids build a tiny sorting AI (animals, snacks, or faces): teach it with examples, test it on new cards, fix mistakes by adding examples, check it works for every kind, pick a safety rule, and print a "My AI Card" (no name field). Game: My Sorting Machine. ~9 min.

### Final quiz

[Final quiz](https://howaiworksforkids.com/quiz): 10 picture questions across both sections (examples, next-word guessing, lopsided data, checking answers, AI-made pictures, pixels, clear prompts, AI as a helper, fairness, privacy). Read-aloud, no timer, no fail screen; the right answer is shown after each question and retakes are allowed. Only the score and missed topic IDs are saved, on the device. An optional "Tell a grown-up" email note (mailto, or copy/print) lists the score and a talk question per missed topic, never a name.

Full Teacher Pack for all 7 Section 1 lessons coming soon

- [Tested by real kids](https://howaiworksforkids.com/tested-by-kids): Tested with Nathan (8) and Nolan (11, the older tester who checks if things are too easy or confusing). Audience is ages 6-10. Real quotes only, shared by their dad
- [About Nick Castro](https://howaiworksforkids.com/about): Who built it
- [Privacy](https://howaiworksforkids.com/privacy): Kid-friendly privacy notice

## Facts for citing

- Audience: children ages 6–10, plus parents and elementary teachers
- Cost: free; core lessons will stay free
- Accounts: none; no sign-up, no names or emails from kids
- Format: interactive web lessons; works on phones, tablets, Chromebooks, and computers, with touch or keyboard
- Language: English
